Mendacious

men-DAY-shus · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Mendacious is not telling the truth; intentionally deceitful.

Reporters eventually exposed the executive's mendacious claims about the company's safety record.

Worked Example

The senator's mendacious testimony unraveled once investigators produced the very documents he had sworn did not exist.

Testimony that unravels once the sworn-nonexistent documents appear is exactly mendacious.

How Mendacious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

deceitful

deceitful: intentionally misleading or dishonest

untruthful

untruthful: not telling the truth

Antonyms

veracious

veracious: habitually speaking the truth

How Strong Is It? — misleading → mendacious → perjurious

misleading vs. mendacious

misleading vs. mendacious: Misleading can happen by accident, through careless wording; mendacious specifically implies a intentional, knowing lie.

perjurious vs. mendacious

perjurious vs. mendacious: Perjurious narrows the lie to sworn, legal testimony under oath, while mendacious describes intentional dishonesty of any kind, in or out of court.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of mendacious.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — mendac

root — mendac: lie, falsehood (Latin (mendax, mendacium))

suffix — -ious

suffix — -ious: possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Mendacious comes from Latin mendax ('lying'), from menda ('fault, blemish') + -ious -- literally 'full of falsehood.'

Use the root in a new word: amend

Use the root in a new word: amend: The same menda ('fault') root, with the prefix e- ('out'), gives us the everyday word amend, literally 'to remove a fault' -- amend and mendacious share this same ancient root for 'fault' or 'flaw,' even though their modern meanings have drifted far apart.
